definition.text: A trade-off is a choice in which you accept less of one thing in return for more of another.

facts.text: Trade-offs arise from limits of many kinds, even simple physics: a full container must lose some items before it can take more.
In economics a trade-off is expressed as the opportunity cost of a choice, the most preferred alternative given up.
Investing in stocks offers higher potential returns with more risk, while bonds are safer but pay less.
Economists often draw trade-offs as a Pareto frontier, such as the production possibilities frontier between two goods.
In environmental management, REDD+ funding faces trade-offs among biodiversity conservation, carbon storage and fair distribution, since maximising one reduces the other two.
Tension between prosperity for all and environmental conservation makes trade-offs necessary in sustainability.

title: Utility

definition.text: In economics, utility is a measure of how satisfied a person is with a particular state of the world.

facts.text: Normatively, utility is a goal to maximise, close to the utilitarian idea of Bentham and Mill; descriptively, it is what people's choices reveal they are pursuing.
A utility function gives each option a number so that preferred options always get higher numbers.
Because utility cannot be observed directly, economists infer it from choices, for example from willingness to pay; Paul Samuelson called these revealed preferences.
Economists separate total utility, the utility of a whole bundle, from marginal utility, the change from one more unit of a good.
Indifference curves plot combinations of goods that give the same satisfaction, and combined with a budget constraint they yield demand curves.
Joan Robinson called utility circular: goods have utility because people want them, and people wanting them shows they have utility.

contested_note: Economists and ethicists disagree about how the normative and descriptive meanings of utility relate, and critics such as Joan Robinson call the concept circular.

definition.text: Cardinal utility treats satisfaction as something that can be measured with numbers, so the size of the differences between options means something.

facts.text: Utility functions are cardinal or ordinal depending on whether they say anything beyond the ranking of options, such as how strong a preference is.
Ordinal utility only ranks options: it can say two ice creams beat one, but not by how much.
Daniel Bernoulli used a logarithmic cardinal utility of money to resolve the St. Petersburg paradox.
